executiveSummary: Chapter 24 examines the full disclosure principle under IFRS, explaining that financial statements must report any facts significant enough to influence an informed reader's judgment. The chapter covers four primary disclosure areas—related-party transactions, subsequent events, segment reporting, and interim reporting—along with the auditor's report, management commentary, fraudulent financial reporting, and (in appendices) financial statement analysis techniques and first-time IFRS adoption procedures.
keyTopics: Full Disclosure Principle: Companies must disclose all material financial facts in the statements, notes, or supplementary information; the IASB has amended IAS 1 to stress that materiality governs what must be disclosed, and that immaterial information can actually reduce usefulness.

Notes to Financial Statements: Notes amplify and explain items in the primary statements; required disclosures include accounting policies (the first or prominent note), significant management judgments and estimation uncertainties, inventory methods, PP&E valuation and depreciation, creditor claims, equity-holder claims, contingencies, fair values, and deferred taxes.

Related-Party Transactions: Transactions where one party can significantly influence another must disclose the nature of the relationship, transaction amounts, outstanding balances and guarantees, provisions for doubtful debts, and bad-debt expenses recognized.

Subsequent Events (Events After the Reporting Period): Adjusted subsequent events (conditions existing at the statement date) require restatement of the financial statements; non-adjusted subsequent events (new conditions arising after the statement date, e.g., fire, acquisition) require footnote disclosure only, not adjustment.

Segment Reporting (IFRS 8 Management Approach): Operating segments are identified based on how management internally organizes and reviews results; a segment is reportable if it meets any of three 10% quantitative thresholds (revenue, profit/loss, assets), and reported segments must collectively cover at least 75% of consolidated external revenue.

Interim Reporting (IAS 34): IFRS requires the discrete approach—each interim period is treated as a separate accounting period using the same policies as annual reports; income taxes use an annualized effective-rate approach, and companies subject to material seasonality must supplement interim reports with 12-month rolling data.

Auditor's Report and Types of Opinions: The auditor issues an unmodified (clean) opinion when statements comply with IFRS; modified opinions include qualified (exception not material enough to invalidate the whole), adverse (exceptions so material that statements as a whole are misstated), and disclaimer (insufficient evidence to form an opinion); Key Audit Matters (KAMs) highlight the most significant judgments in the audit.

Fraudulent Financial Reporting: Defined as intentional or reckless conduct resulting in materially misleading statements; common causes include weak internal controls, management pressure for short-term results, and complex transactions subject to subjective judgment; auditing standards require explicit fraud-risk assessment.

importantDefinitions.Full Disclosure Principle: The requirement to report any financial facts significant enough to influence the judgment of an informed reader of the financial statements.
importantDefinitions.Accounting Policies: The specific principles, bases, conventions, rules, and practices applied by a company in preparing and presenting financial statements.
importantDefinitions.Adjusted Subsequent Event: An event occurring after the statement of financial position date but before authorization for issuance that provides additional evidence about conditions existing at the statement date; requires adjustment to the financial statements.
importantDefinitions.Non-Adjusted Subsequent Event: An event occurring after the statement of financial position date that provides evidence about conditions that did not exist at that date; requires footnote disclosure but not adjustment of the financial statements.
importantDefinitions.Operating Segment: A component of an enterprise that earns revenues and incurs expenses, whose results are regularly reviewed by the chief operating decision-maker, and for which discrete financial information is available.
importantDefinitions.Management Approach (Segment Reporting): The IFRS method of identifying reportable segments based on how company management organizes the business internally for decision-making and resource allocation.
importantDefinitions.Discrete Approach (Interim Reporting): The view that each interim period is a separate accounting period; expenses are recognized as incurred without anticipating or deferring costs based on expected annual results. Required by IFRS.
importantDefinitions.Integral Approach (Interim Reporting): The view that an interim period is an integral part of the annual period; costs are allocated among periods based on expected annual activity. Required under U.S. GAAP.
importantDefinitions.Key Audit Matters (KAMs): Matters that, in the auditor's professional judgment, were of most significance in the audit of the current period financial statements; must be described in the auditor's report.
importantDefinitions.Fraudulent Financial Reporting: Intentional or reckless conduct, whether act or omission, that results in materially misleading financial statements.
importantDefinitions.Safe Harbor Rule: A regulatory protection that shields a company from liability for an erroneous financial forecast, provided the forecast was prepared on a reasonable basis and disclosed in good faith.
importantDefinitions.Alternative (Management) Performance Mea: Financial metrics developed by management that are not defined solely by IFRS (e.g., constant-currency revenue growth, free cash flow); must be reconciled to the nearest IFRS measure when disclosed.

accountingTreatments: Related-party disclosures (IAS 24): No special measurement rule — amounts are reported at the values agreed between the parties; however, IFRS requires disclosure of the nature of the relationship, transaction amounts, outstanding balances, and any bad-debt provisions so users can assess whether arm's-length terms were absent.

Adjusted subsequent events: The company adjusts the financial statements before issuance. Example — a customer bankruptcy discovered after year-end but stemming from pre-year-end insolvency: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts / Cr Accounts Receivable for the estimated uncollectible balance.

Non-adjusted subsequent events: No adjusting entry is made; instead, the company discloses in a footnote the nature and estimated financial effect (e.g., a post-year-end plant fire, a major acquisition, or a new share issue).

Segment reporting measurement: Segment profit/loss and assets are measured on the same basis used in internal management reports, which need not conform to IFRS consolidation policies; companies reconcile total segment revenues, profits, and assets to the consolidated IFRS totals.

Interim income taxes: Tax expense each quarter is based on the best estimate of the weighted-average annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date pre-tax income; the accrual is adjusted in subsequent quarters if the estimated annual rate changes.

First-time IFRS adoption (IFRS 1): Opening IFRS statement of financial position adjustments are recorded through retained earnings. Example — capitalizing previously expensed development costs of €500,000: Dr Intangible Assets €500,000 / Cr Retained Earnings €500,000. A warranty not recognized under prior GAAP: Dr Retained Earnings €100,000 / Cr Warranty Liability €100,000.
criticalFormulas: 10% Revenue Threshold for Reportable Segments: Segment Revenue >= 0.10 × Total Combined Revenue of ALL Segments. Example: Total combined revenue = €2,150k; threshold = €215k; any segment with revenue >= €215k is potentially reportable.

10% Profit/Loss Threshold: |Segment Profit or Loss| >= 0.10 × MAX(|Sum of all profitable segments|, |Sum of all loss segments|). Example: Sum of profitable segments = €90k; threshold = €9k; a segment with operating profit of €10k or a loss of €10k meets this test.

10% Assets Threshold: Segment Identifiable Assets >= 0.10 × Total Combined Assets of ALL Segments. Example: Total combined assets = €970k; threshold = €97k; any segment with assets >= €97k is potentially reportable.

75% Adequacy Test: Sum of External Revenue of All Reportable Segments >= 0.75 × Total Consolidated External Revenue. Example: Reportable segments' external revenue = €2,000k; 0.75 × €2,150k = €1,612.5k; €2,000k >= €1,612.5k, so the test is met.

Annualized Interim Tax Rate: Interim Income Tax Expense = (Estimated Weighted-Average Annual Effective Tax Rate) × Year-to-Date Pre-Tax Income. Example: Estimated annual rate = 30%; Q1 pre-tax income = €100k; Q1 tax accrual = 0.30 × €100k = €30k.

disclosurePresentationNotes: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies must be presented as the first note (or in a prominent separate section) and must include: basis of preparation, all significant policies (depreciation methods, inventory costing, revenue recognition), key management judgments, and major sources of estimation uncertainty with the nature and carrying amount of affected assets/liabilities.

Segment disclosures (IFRS 8) must include: general description of how segments were identified, segment revenues from external customers and intersegment transfers, segment profit/loss with interest, depreciation, unusual items, and tax; segment assets and liabilities; and a reconciliation of segment totals to consolidated IFRS totals. If a single customer accounts for 10% or more of company revenue, that fact and the revenue amount by segment must be disclosed.

Subsequent events note must state the nature of each event and provide an estimate of its financial effect; if estimation is not practicable, that fact must be stated. The authorization date of the financial statements must also be disclosed so users know the end of the subsequent-events period.

First-time IFRS adopters must present at minimum three statements of financial position, two of each other primary statement, and reconciliations of equity and total comprehensive income from previous GAAP to IFRS at both the transition date and the end of the comparative period, with explanatory notes for each material adjustment.
potentialPitfalls: Confusing adjusted vs. non-adjusted subsequent events: Students often adjust financial statements for all post-year-end events. Only events that provide additional evidence about conditions existing at the statement date require adjustment; events arising from entirely new conditions after year-end require disclosure only, not adjusting entries.

Misapplying the segment 10% tests: The profit/loss test uses the greater of the absolute total of profitable segments OR the absolute total of loss segments as the denominator — NOT the net profit figure; ignoring this can cause loss segments (like a €2k loss in the example) to be incorrectly excluded when the company has large profitable segments.

Treating interim periods as integral under IFRS: Under IFRS the discrete approach applies, meaning expenses (including fixed costs like advertising) are recognized when incurred, not allocated proportionally over the year based on annual sales projections; allocating fixed non-manufacturing costs to quarters based on expected annual sales activity is an integral approach and is not permitted under IAS 34.
